questions.q: In « le roi », what sound do the letters oi make?
questions.why: oi is always one sound, "wah": le roi, la joie, le mois, le doigt. It is never sounded out letter by letter.

questions.q: « le gâteau », « l'eau », « aussitôt » — what do eau, au and ô have in common?
choices: They are all a closed, rounded "oh"
questions.why: au, eau and ô all spell the same closed /o/. Different spellings, one sound — which is why combinations beat letters in French.

questions.q: How many syllables does « maïs » (corn) have?
choices: Two, but the second is silent
questions.why: The tréma means "pronounce this vowel separately", so it breaks ai apart. « mais » (but) is one syllable; « maïs » is two, and the tréma is the only thing separating them.

questions.q: Is the vowel of « bonne » nasal?
choices: No — the doubled n cancels the nasal and is pronounced
Yes, but shorter than in « bon »
No, and the n is silent too
questions.why: A vowel is nasal only when a single m/n closes the syllable. Double the consonant, or put a vowel after it, and the nasal switches off: bon becomes bonne, fin becomes fine, l'an becomes l'année.

questions.q: In which of these do the letters ill NOT make a y-sound?
questions.why: Four common words keep ill as a plain "eel": mille, la ville, tranquille, le village. Everywhere else ill is a y-sound, so la fille and la ville do not rhyme.

questions.q: How is the ending of the adverb « évidemment » pronounced?
questions.why: -emment is always said -amment. It matters because every adjective in -ent builds its adverb this way: fréquemment, récemment, évidemment.

questions.q: Add the missing accent: « la fete » (the party, the celebration).
questions.why: The circumflex here marks an s that fell out of the word centuries ago (compare English "feast"). It sounds like è, the open vowel of English "fair".

questions.q: « mais » means "but". Rewrite it so it becomes the two-syllable word for corn.
questions.why: Only the tréma changes: it splits ai into two separate vowels, ma-ees.

questions.q: « bon » has a nasal vowel. Write the form ending in -ne, where the n is actually heard.
questions.why: Doubling the n restores the ordinary vowel and makes the consonant audible. Same pattern: fin becomes fine, un an becomes une année.

questions.q: « le frein » (the brake) has a nasal vowel. Write the -er verb built on it, meaning "to brake".
questions.why: A vowel now follows the n, so the nasal disappears: frein is nasal, freiner is not. Spelling barely changes; the sound changes completely.
Two traps in one short word: oi is "wah", and on is a nasal whose n you never actually pronounce.
ou is the "oo" of "food", and -eille is a y-sound: boo-tay-y. Nothing here is sounded letter by letter.

questions.q: Say this out loud. Round your lips hard: this is not "roo".
questions.why: u is the sound English does not have: say "ee", keep your tongue exactly there, then round your lips. « la roue » (the wheel) is the back-of-the-mouth "oo"; « la rue » (the street) is not.

questions.q: Say this out loud — the ending is a single y-sound, and the u in the middle is the tight French u.
questions.why: -euil is one rounded y-sound, and the u before it is the front-rounded u of « la rue ». Squirrel is a good stress test for the whole chapter.

questions.q: Name the four common words in which the letters ill do NOT make a y-sound, and say what they sound like instead.
a: mille, la ville, tranquille, le village — in these, ill is a plain "eel" sound, so la ville does not rhyme with la fille. There is no rule behind it; the words are simply old.
questions.why: The -ille rule is otherwise very reliable, so the exceptions are worth holding as a closed list of four rather than guessing each time.
